title: The quiet successor's words
hook: Guru Angad's saloks, short verses, sit inside the Vars

segments.voice: Yesterday we closed Guru Nanak's longer teachings and saw the name Nanak carry on into the next voice. Your line was nanak's way. Which teaching did you choose, and did you tell anyone? Day one thousand one hundred seventy-seven.

Guru Nanak's voice fills raga after raga of the Guru Granth Sahib, hymn after long hymn. Go looking for the second Guru's, and it arrives another way: in small pieces, a few lines each, tucked into the Vars, the ballads, between the stanzas. Each one carries a small heading: Mahala two, the second voice. This is Guru Angad, the disciple Guru Nanak chose to follow him, and in the stories about him he's a man of few words and much service. Today we start a short stretch on his words, and the first thing to notice is how small each one is.
screen: `NOT LONG HYMNS.` → `SMALL PIECES IN THE BALLADS.` → `MAHALA TWO: THE SECOND VOICE.`

segments.voice: A salok is a short verse of a few lines, and in the Vars they're set before the longer stanzas, like a sharp word before a speech. Guru Angad's verses live there, in that small form. So what can a few lines hold? Here's one of his saloks from the Var in Majh, the same ballad we closed a few days ago, in paraphrase. To see without eyes. To hear without ears. To walk without feet. To work without hands. To speak without a tongue. This way, a person dies while still alive. Nanak, recognize the divine order, and meet your Master. Notice the signature: Nanak, even though this is the second Guru speaking. That's the name carrying on. And notice the form. Five short pictures, each one impossible on its face, stacked one after another. Then one line to turn them: this is dying while alive. Then one line to point the way: recognize the hukam. Some Sikh teachers read it as a picture of living without ego: seeing, hearing, working and speaking, but no longer driven by the self that wants to own it all. The verse doesn't explain that. It leaves the five pictures hanging and lets you work them out. That's the quiet successor's style. He doesn't need a long hymn. He gives you something small and dense, the way a seed is small, and lets it open in you over a long time. Few words. And deep. That's today's line.
screen: `A SALOK: A FEW SHARP LINES.` · `SEE WITHOUT EYES, WALK WITHOUT FEET.` · `DYING WHILE ALIVE.` · `SMALL, DENSE, LIKE A SEED.` · then, large: `FEW WORDS, DEEP.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read one salok of Mahala two. You've just heard one. In the sit, take only one of its pictures, whichever one stays with you. Hear without ears, maybe, or work without hands. Let the breath slow and keep that one phrase in front of you. Don't try to solve it. Just turn it over, the way you'd turn a stone in your palm. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
The quiet successor's words. Guru Angad's saloks, marked Mahala two, a few dense lines each, set inside the ballads of the Granth. Today's word.
Your line: few words, deep. Say one thing today in fewer words than you normally would, and let it land. Day one thousand one hundred seventy-seven.

howItsDone: Sikhs hear Guru Angad's saloks when the Vars are sung in kirtan, especially Asa di Var in the morning, where his saloks sit beside those of Guru Nanak.

fork.reveal: it doesn't explain them; it names them dying while alive, then points to recognizing the hukam.

what a scholar hears: the Majh ki Var salok of seeing without eyes, signed Nanak under Mahala two, a picture of dying while alive.
